back: Materials developed to have specific properties that improve on existing materials.
Materials that react to an external stimulus such as temperature, light or pressure.
Very stiff, high tensile strength and lightweight; usually used in a composite — racing bikes, F1 cars, aerospace.
A strong, heat-resistant synthetic fibre, about five times stronger than steel for its weight — protective vests.
Glass fibres in a polymer resin, giving high compressive and tensile strength — boats, car body panels, water slides.
Trade name for extruded polystyrene foam (blue modelling foam) — easy to cut and shape. Not the same as white expanded polystyrene.
A dense foam layer between two thin card faces — used for mounting and architectural models; can be laser cut.
A rubbery material that is an electrical insulator normally but becomes a conductor when compressed — used as switches.
Change colour in UV light — self-darkening spectacles and glazing on tall buildings.
Change colour with temperature — baby spoons, bottles and bath toys.
Nickel-titanium alloy that returns to its original shape when heated — spectacle frames and dental braces.
A polymer that becomes malleable at 62°C, can be shaped by hand and reheated many times.
